190.title: Toldot: Esau's tears (Genesis 27:34–38)
190.hook: the tradition takes Esau's bitter cry seriously; his pain is written down
190.howItsDone: Jewish teaching often turns to the suffering of the other side: at the Passover seder, it's a custom to spill drops of wine as each plague on Egypt is named, and the midrash on Esau's cry is taught alongside this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacob in goatskin, and a blind father feeling the gap. Your line was voice and hands the same. Today, the brother who comes home too late.

Nobody films the losing team's locker room. The cameras are down the hall, with the champagne, and the kid on the bench with a towel over his head stays off the screen. Plenty of stories follow the winner out the door. Jacob has just walked out of his father's tent with the blessing. Minutes later, Esau walks in, sweaty from the hunt, carrying the meal he cooked, saying: sit up, father, and eat, so you can bless me. The Torah stays in that room.
screen: `THE LOSING TEAM'S LOCKER ROOM.` → `JACOB WALKS OUT.` → `ESAU WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Isaac asks: who are you? I am your son, your firstborn, Esau. And the text says Isaac trembled, a great trembling, beyond measure. Who was it, then, who came before you? I've blessed him, and he will stay blessed. Esau cries out, a great and bitter cry. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Bless me, even me also, O my father." He asks again: "Hast thou but one blessing, my father?" And Esau lifts up his voice and weeps. Stop there for a moment. This is the brother the story didn't choose, the one Rebekah didn't favor. The Torah could have skipped this scene. Instead it gives us his words, twice, and his tears. Isaac does give him a blessing, a harder one: you'll live by your sword, and serve your brother, and one day you'll break his yoke from your neck. The rabbis didn't look away either. An old midrash says Jacob made Esau cry out one bitter cry, and that cry was repaid generations later, in the book of Esther, when Mordecai too cried out with a loud and bitter cry. That pain was not forgotten. It counted. There's a thread in Jewish tradition of taking the other side's suffering seriously, even the side you're told was not chosen. At the Passover seder, there's a custom of spilling drops of wine from the cup as the plagues on Egypt are named, and one common explanation is that a full cup of joy shouldn't ignore someone else's pain. The winner gets the blessing. But the Torah writes down the loser's tears.

segments.voice: Think of a time you won something, a job, an argument, a game, a place, and then of the person on the other side. Where were they that night, and what did it feel like to walk into the room too late? You don't have to give anything back; just let their loss be real to you for a minute.

191.title: Vayetze: leaving town (Genesis 28:10)
191.hook: Rashi: when a good person leaves a town, its beauty leaves with them
191.howItsDone: Vayetze is read in synagogues each late autumn, and Rashi's commentary is commonly printed beside the Torah text for study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esau's bitter cry, bless me, even me also. Your line was the loser's tears count. Today, a new portion, and Jacob on the run.

A coworker retires on a Friday. The one who remembered birthdays, who made the bad coffee a little better, who laughed at everything. On Monday it's the same building, the same desks. But something has gone out of the place, and it stays gone for weeks. This week's portion is called Vayetze, and he went out. Esau is furious and wants his brother dead, so Rebekah and Isaac send Jacob away, to her family in Haran. He leaves home with nothing but a staff.
screen: `THE OFFICE AFTER SHE RETIRED.` → `VAYETZE: AND HE WENT OUT.` → `JACOB LEAVES WITH A STAFF.`

segments.voice: The portion opens with a short verse: Jacob went out from Beer-sheba, and went toward Haran. Rashi, the medieval teacher from France, read it slowly and asked a simple question. The verse could have said only that Jacob went toward Haran. Why mention that he left Beer-sheba at all? The words should earn their place. Rashi's answer, drawn from an old midrash, is lovely. When a good person leaves a place, it makes an impression. While they live in a town, they are its glory, its brightness, its beauty. When they go, the glory, the brightness and the beauty go with them. Now notice who it's about. Jacob, right now, isn't a hero. He's just deceived his father and fled his brother. And still, the rabbis say, Beer-sheba was a little dimmer the morning he left. Rashi even asks: but Isaac was still there, wasn't he? And he answers, more or less: one good person is not the same as two. Every good person counts, and one leaving still leaves a gap. It turns a familiar idea around, that places make people: a good neighborhood, a good school. Rashi is saying the opposite is at least as true. People make places. The quiet ones, too, who hold the door and know everyone's kids' names. You often don't know what they were until the morning after they've gone.

segments.voice: Picture a place you're in every week: your street, your work, your building, your prayer community, your gym. Now picture it without the one person who makes it a little warmer, and feel what would go out of the room. Hold their face in mind for a moment, with gratitude.

192.title: Vayetze: and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)
192.hook: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not"
192.howItsDone: Jews often call God HaMakom, the Place, and the phrase appears in the traditional words of comfort said to mourners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayetze: Jacob leaving Beer-sheba, and a town a little dimmer. Your line was people make places. Tonight, Jacob sleeps outside.

The bus stop you stand at every morning. The hallway between the kitchen and the bedroom. The stretch of highway you drive without seeing. Nobody expects anything holy there. Jacob, running from his brother, comes to an ordinary place as the sun goes down. No town, no inn. He takes one of the stones lying around, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground to sleep. Nothing marks the spot.
screen: `THE BUS STOP. THE HALLWAY.` → `SUNSET, NOWHERE IN PARTICULAR.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: Jacob dreams. A ladder, a sulam, is set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels of God are going up and coming down on it. Up first, then down, the rabbis noticed. God stands beside him and makes a promise: this land, children like the dust of the earth, and I will be with you and keep you wherever you go, and bring you back. Jacob wakes up and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." He's afraid, and he says the place is full of awe: nothing less than the house of God, the gate of heaven. He names it Beth-el, house of God. The text adds, almost dryly, that the town used to be called Luz. An ordinary name for an ordinary place. Listen to that line again. And I knew it not. The Hebrew for I here is anochi, the longer of two Hebrew words for I, and some Hasidic teachers played with it. Why didn't Jacob know God was there? Because of the anochi: he was full of himself, his fear, his plans, his running. The rabbis also gave God a name from stories like this: HaMakom, the Place. A midrash says God is the place of the world, but the world is not God's place. There's no spot on earth too plain for it. In Jacob's own words, God was already there; the dream didn't bring him. What changed was that he woke up and noticed.

segments.voice: Wherever you are right now, the car, a bench, the kitchen floor, look around slowly, as if you'd just woken from Jacob's dream, and find what you've stopped seeing: the light on the wall, the sound of the street, the fact that you're breathing at all. If you pray, you can say Jacob's line quietly. If not, just let the place be more than it was a minute ago.

193.title: Vayetze: a tenth (Genesis 28:20–22)
193.hook: Jacob vows a tenth of all he is given, a root of Jewish giving
193.howItsDone: Some Jews give ma'aser kesafim, a tenth of their income, to tzedakah, often keeping a running account of what they owe to it; the biblical tithes of produce are still set aside in a symbolic way in Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a ladder in a plain place, and Jacob waking up. Your line was and I knew it not. This morning, Jacob makes a promise.

Look at your last paycheck, or your last grocery receipt, or the hours in your week. Somewhere in there is the question every budget asks: what's mine, and what do I give away? Jacob, the morning after his dream, owns almost nothing: a staff, the clothes he slept in, and the stone that was his pillow. He sets that stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and makes a vow. The vow is about money he doesn't have yet.
screen: `WHAT'S MINE, WHAT DO I GIVE?` → `A STAFF AND A STONE.` → `A VOW ABOUT MONEY HE DOESN'T HAVE.`

segments.voice: Jacob's vow is a list of plain needs. If God will be with me, and keep me on this road, and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and I come back to my father's house in peace, then this stone will be God's house. Then the last line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and of all that Thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto Thee." In Hebrew it's doubled: aser a'asrenu, I will tenth it, a tenth. A promise said twice, for emphasis. Notice where he starts: not from surplus, from zero. He's promising a tenth of whatever he'll someday have, before he has any of it. He isn't the first. His grandfather Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils of war to Melchizedek, a priest-king. Later, the Torah turns the tenth into law: a tithe of the harvest, shared with the Levite, the stranger, the orphan and the widow. The word for tithe is ma'aser, from the Hebrew for ten, and later Jewish custom also speaks of ma'aser kesafim, a tenth of money. Maimonides, the great medieval teacher, wrote that giving a fifth of what you have is the finest way, a tenth is the ordinary way, and less than that is a stingy eye. The Talmud makes a gentle pun, too. Aser, to tithe, sounds like osher, wealth: give a tenth so that you'll become rich. The same passage even calls this the one place where testing God is allowed, citing the prophet Malachi. Either way, the pun ties giving and wealth together in one sound.
screen: `IF GOD WILL BE WITH ME…` · `ASER A'ASRENU: A TENTH, TWICE.` · `ABRAHAM, THEN THE HARVEST, THEN MONEY.` · `A FIFTH, A TENTH, A STINGY EYE.` · then, large: `I WILL SURELY GIVE THE TENTH.`

segments.voice: Choose something to set a tenth of aside; it doesn't have to be money. A tenth of your day is about two and a half hours, a tenth of an hour is six minutes, or a tenth of your pantry or this week's paycheck. Picture setting that tenth apart for someone who needs it more than you do, and notice how it feels to decide before you spend.
Ma'aser. A tenth, a tithe: what Jacob vowed with nothing in his pocket, and a root of Jewish giving ever since.

194.title: Vayetze: the stone on the well (Genesis 29:9–11)
194.hook: Jacob rolls away a stone meant for many shepherds, then weeps
194.howItsDone: Jacob and Rachel's meeting at the well is read each late autumn in Vayetze, and the well is a recurring meeting place in the Torah's love stories, from Rebekah to Rachel to Moses and Zipporah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ma'aser, Jacob's vow of a tenth, made with nothing in his pocket. Your line was give a tenth. Today, Jacob arrives.

You've heard the stories. A mother lifts a car off her child. A tired dad carries a sleeping kid up three flights of stairs without noticing. Love does strange things to a body. Jacob, after weeks on the road, comes to a well in a field in the east. Three flocks of sheep lie beside it, waiting. On the well's mouth sits a great stone, so heavy, the shepherds tell him, that they can only move it when all the shepherds gather. Then a young woman walks up with her father's sheep.
screen: `LOVE DOES STRANGE THINGS.` → `A WELL, A GREAT STONE.` → `A YOUNG WOMAN WITH HER SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Jacob asks the shepherds why they're waiting. It's the middle of the day: water the sheep and go back to pasture. We can't, they say, not until all the flocks are gathered and together we roll the stone from the well's mouth. That's the rule of this well. It takes everyone. While they're still talking, Rachel arrives, the daughter of Laban, his mother's brother. She's a shepherd, the text says; she tends her father's flock herself. Jacob sees her. He goes up, alone, and rolls the stone off the mouth of the well, the stone that took all the shepherds together. Rashi says he moved it as easily as pulling a cork from a bottle, to show how strong he was. He waters his uncle's whole flock. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept." Why weep, at the happiest moment? The text doesn't say. The rabbis offered answers. One midrash says he wept because he came empty-handed: his grandfather's servant had arrived at a well like this one with ten camels loaded with gifts, and Jacob had nothing to give. Rashi also says he foresaw that Rachel would not be buried beside him. Maybe it was just everything at once: the road, the fear, the relief of family, love at first sight. Strength and tears in the same scene, and the Torah doesn't make him choose. Love made him strong enough to move a stone meant for many, and soft enough to cry in front of strangers.
screen: `IT TAKES ALL THE SHEPHERDS.` · `RACHEL, A SHEPHERD HERSELF.` · `ONE MAN ROLLS THE STONE.` · `WHY WEEP?` · then, large: `AND JACOB KISSED RACHEL, AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of one stone in your life right now, something that feels too heavy for you alone: a task, a conversation, a long week. Then think of someone you love, and why you'd want to do it for them, and feel whether the stone gets any lighter. If some tears come with it, let them; Jacob had both.
Vayetze. And he went out: the portion where Jacob, alone, rolls a stone meant for many, for Rachel, and then weeps.
Your line: love moves stones. And it leaves room for tears. Day one hundred ninety-four, done.

195.title: Vayetze: angels at the border (Genesis 32:2–3)
195.hook: the portion opens and closes with angels at the edges of the journey
195.howItsDone: Jews mark thresholds with blessings and customs, from the mezuzah on the doorpost to the traveler's prayer said at the start of a journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stone meant for many, moved by one man in love. Your line was love moves stones. Today, twenty years later, Jacob heads home.

A first day at a new job. The drive home from the hospital with a newborn. The last box carried out of an apartment. Some days are thresholds, the strip at the foot of a doorway, and they don't run like ordinary days. Jacob arrived in Haran with a staff. Twenty years later, he leaves with two wives, Leah and Rachel, eleven sons and a daughter, flocks, servants, and a complicated relationship with his father-in-law, Laban. Laban chases him, they argue, they make a covenant, and they part. Jacob is finally going home.
screen: `THRESHOLDS FEEL DIFFERENT.` → `TWENTY YEARS IN HARAN.` → `JACOB HEADS HOME.`

segments.voice: This portion is built like a pair of bookends. It opened with Jacob leaving home, sleeping on a stone, dreaming of angels going up and down a ladder. And it closes, twenty years later, like this, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him." He sees them and says, this is God's camp, and he names the place Mahanaim, which means two camps. Angels at the start of the journey, angels at the end, and in between a whole life: marriages, children, hard work, being cheated, and learning to hold his own. The rabbis noticed the bookends and asked what they meant. Rashi, back at the ladder, has a striking picture. Why do the angels go up first and then come down? Because the angels who had been with Jacob in the land of Israel went up at the border, and a new group of angels came down to go with him outside it. A changing of the guard. And here at Mahanaim, Rashi says the same thing happens in reverse: the angels who went with him abroad and the angels of the land meet at the border, to hand him over. Two camps, one traveler. The Torah itself only tells us angels met him; it doesn't say what they did or said. But Rashi's picture is easy to carry: Jacob doesn't cross that border alone. At the edge, one company lets go of him, and another is waiting.

segments.voice: Think of what's starting or finishing in your life right now: a new job, a child leaving, a friendship changing, the end of a season. Picture yourself standing at that border, and notice who is letting go of you on one side and who is waiting on the other. Maybe a person; maybe, if you believe it, something more.

196.title: Vayishlach: too small (Genesis 32:11)
196.hook: Jacob prays "I am not worthy of all the mercies"
196.carry: too small for all this kindness
196.howItsDone: Some teachers compare the shape of Jacob's prayer, praise and thanks first and then a request, to the Amidah, the central Jewish prayer, which opens by naming the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahanaim, two camps. Your line was angels at every border. This week: Esau's tears, a town dimmer when Jacob left, a ladder in a plain place, a tenth, a stone moved by love, and angels at the edges. Today, a new portion.

You're about to see someone you wronged a long time ago. A sibling, an ex, an old friend. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times. Then you hear they're coming, and they're bringing a crowd. This week's portion is called Vayishlach, and he sent. Jacob sends messengers ahead to his brother Esau, twenty years after he took his blessing. They come back with news: Esau is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.
screen: `THE PERSON YOU WRONGED.` → `VAYISHLACH: AND HE SENT.` → `FOUR HUNDRED MEN.`

segments.voice: The Torah says Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. Two words, and Rashi says they mean two different fears: afraid he'd be killed, and distressed that he might have to kill. He splits his people into two camps, so that if one is attacked, the other can escape. Then he prays, and it's worth hearing how it goes. He begins with God's names: God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac. He reminds God of the promise: you told me, go home, and I'll do you good. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am not worthy of all the mercies" and all the faithfulness you've shown your servant. In Hebrew it's one word: katonti. I am small. I've become too small for all of this. With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, he says, and now I've become two camps. Think about who's saying this: Jacob, rich now, with a big family, a man who's worked his way through twenty years. His first move in danger isn't to list what he deserves. It's to say: I'm small, and I've been given so much. Only after that does he ask. Save me, please, from my brother's hand, because I'm afraid of him. Plain fear, said out loud. Some teachers hold up this prayer as a model: gratitude first, honesty about being small, and then a direct request. Being small, here, isn't shame. It's what makes the kindness visible.
screen: `AFRAID AND DISTRESSED.` · `GOD OF MY FATHERS, YOU PROMISED.` · `KATONTI: I AM SMALL.` · `SAVE ME: I AM AFRAID.` · then, large: `I AM NOT WORTHY OF ALL THE MERCIES.`

segments.voice: Think of what you have that you once didn't, people, a roof, a skill, another morning, and let yourself feel small next to it, the good kind of small. Then name, plainly, the thing you're afraid of right now. If you pray, you can use Jacob's words, I am not worthy of all the mercies, and then ask for help; if you don't, just hold both, the gifts and the fear.
Vayishlach. And he sent: the portion where Jacob, afraid of meeting his brother, prays that he's too small for all the kindness he's been shown.

Rashi reads afraid and distressed as two different fears
afraid he'd be killed; distressed that he might have to kill.
Jacob hid his fear in the prayer
he says it plainly: save me from my brother, because I'm afraid of him.

fork.setup: your brother is coming with four hundred men. you're Jacob. you pray. how do you begin?
options: say you're too small for all the kindness you've had.
ask right away to be saved.
fork.reveal: Jacob begins with God's promise and his own smallness: I am not worthy of all the mercies. only then does he ask for help.

original.note: Hebrew: I am small. Jacob's word for being unworthy of all God's kindness.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jacob putting himself down.
what it means: gratitude and honesty about being small, before asking for help.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 32:10–13 is taught by some as a model of prayer: praise, thanks, then request.
guess: and he sent, messengers sent ahead
and he feared, Jacob's dread of Esau
and he divided, splitting into two camps
